subject: ela
intro: Each item gives you two texts in different forms, usually a poem and a prose passage, that explore the same theme or topic. Read both closely. Then analyze how each form shapes the way the theme reaches the reader, and name a real similarity or difference supported by both texts. Answer in complete sentences, and point to specific evidence in each text.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "First Day"
New shoes too stiff, new hallway too wide,
my name on a list I did not choose.
I swallow the lump, I lift my chin,
and walk in anyway, new shoes.

STORY: Tomas stood at the edge of the cafeteria, tray shaking in his hands. He had moved to this town three weeks ago, and the long tables still felt like a wall. He searched for a single open seat that did not already belong to a group. Then a boy with a green backpack waved him over and slid down the bench to make room. Tomas let out a breath he did not know he had been holding and sat.

Both texts explore the same theme. State the shared theme, then explain how each text's form delivers it differently.
items.answer: Both texts explore the courage it takes to face a new and unfamiliar place. The poem delivers it through compressed, first-person images and short lines, such as 'I swallow the lump, I lift my chin,' which make the speaker's effort feel sudden and inward. The story delivers it through events over time, showing Tomas frozen with a shaking tray until another student makes room, so the reader feels the relief through what happens.

steps: Identify the shared theme: both texts show a young person finding the courage to enter an unfamiliar place, the poem on a first day of school and the story in a new cafeteria.
The poem uses a tight first-person voice and short lines packed with physical images ('swallow the lump,' 'lift my chin') to compress the feeling into a quick, inner moment.
The story uses a sequence of events, the shaking tray, the search for a seat, the boy who waves him over, so the same theme builds gradually through plot.
A complete answer names the shared theme of courage in a new place and contrasts the poem's compressed imagery with the story's unfolding events.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Tide"
The sea takes back what the sand has lent,
grain by grain, it does not ask.
What we build by noon is gone by night,
yet still we kneel to the task.

STORY: Every summer Nana planted the same flower bed, and every winter the frost killed it. "Why bother," Liam asked, "if it just dies?" Nana pressed a seed into his palm. "Because the bother is the point," she said. "I do not plant for the flowers that last. I plant for the planting." Liam looked at the seed, then knelt and pushed it into the cold soil beside hers.

Both texts treat the same idea about effort. Name one way the two texts are similar in the message they send, and support it with evidence from each.
items.answer: Both texts send the message that the effort itself has value even when the result does not last. The poem says 'What we build by noon is gone by night, yet still we kneel to the task,' showing people keep working though the sea erases it. The story echoes this when Nana says 'the bother is the point' and 'I plant for the planting,' showing she values the act over the lasting flower.

steps: Find the shared message: both texts argue that effort is worthwhile even when what we make is temporary.
Pull poem evidence: 'What we build by noon is gone by night, yet still we kneel to the task' shows continued effort despite loss.
Pull story evidence: Nana's line 'the bother is the point' and 'I plant for the planting' shows the same idea about valuing the effort.
A complete answer states the shared message and quotes a line from each text that supports it.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Storm Watch"
Thunder is only a bully of sound,
big in the dark, gone by the dawn.
I count the seconds, one, two, three,
until the loud thing moves along.

STORY: When the power went out, eight-year-old Priya climbed into the closet with her flashlight and a blanket. Her older brother Sam did not laugh. He crawled in beside her and started a card game by flashlight. "Storms are louder in a closet," he said, "so let us make our own noise." They shuffled and dealt and laughed until the thunder seemed far away, just background to the game.

Both texts show a way of handling fear. Explain how each text's form shapes the way it presents coping with fear.
items.answer: The poem's short, steady lines and the speaker's counting ('one, two, three') turn coping into a calm inner ritual that the reader experiences from the inside. The story's form uses two characters and dialogue, so coping becomes something shared, shown through Sam crawling in and saying 'let us make our own noise.' The poem makes the reader feel one mind steadying itself, while the story shows fear eased by company.

steps: Identify the shared topic: both texts show a character coping with fear, in the poem a storm, in the story a storm during a blackout.
Analyze the poem's form: a single first-person voice and the counting 'one, two, three' present coping as a private, internal strategy.
Analyze the story's form: dialogue and two characters present coping as something shared, with Sam's company and the card game.
A complete answer links each form feature to its effect: the poem's inward voice versus the story's shared action.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "The Loan"
You gave me your coat in the freezing rain
and wore the cold so I would not.
I never paid that kindness back,
but I have spent it, lot by lot.

STORY: Mr. Alvarez had once helped Dana's mother find work when no one else would. Years later Dana noticed a new family struggling in the apartment downstairs. She left bags of groceries at their door without a note. When her mother asked why, Dana shrugged. "Mr. Alvarez never let us thank him," she said. "He just told us to pass it on someday. So I am."

Both texts develop the same theme about kindness. Name the theme and explain how each form develops it.
items.answer: Both texts develop the theme that kindness is repaid by passing it on to others rather than returning it directly. The poem develops it through metaphor and compression, calling the kindness a loan the speaker has 'spent, lot by lot.' The story develops it through plot and dialogue, showing Dana leave groceries and explain 'He just told us to pass it on someday. So I am.' The poem suggests the idea in images while the story shows it in action.

steps: Name the shared theme: kindness is best repaid by passing it forward to someone new.
Poem development: it uses the metaphor of a loan and the line 'I have spent it, lot by lot' to suggest the kindness moving outward.
Story development: it uses events and Dana's dialogue 'pass it on someday. So I am' to make the same idea concrete.
A complete answer names the theme and contrasts the poem's metaphor with the story's plot and dialogue.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Summit"
The mountain did not want me there.
It threw down ice and held its breath.
I did not climb to beat the peak,
I climbed to learn how far I had left.

STORY: The science fair judges had already moved past Wendy's table when she realized her display had a flaw. She could have hidden it. Instead she raised her hand and explained the error to the head judge, even though it might cost her the ribbon. She did not win. But walking home, she felt taller than she had all week, because she had told the truth when it was hard.

Both texts explore the idea of success. State one clear difference in how each text treats what counts as success.
items.answer: Both texts treat success as something other than winning, but they emphasize different forms of it. The poem's speaker says 'I did not climb to beat the peak, I climbed to learn how far I had left,' so success there means self-knowledge and growth. The story shows Wendy choose honesty over the ribbon and feel 'taller than she had all week,' so success there means integrity. The poem stresses learning about oneself while the story stresses doing the right thing.

steps: Identify the shared topic: both texts redefine success as something deeper than a victory.
Poem's version: 'I climbed to learn how far I had left' defines success as growth and self-knowledge.
Story's version: Wendy gives up the ribbon for honesty and feels taller, defining success as integrity.
A complete answer names both as redefining success but contrasts self-knowledge with honesty as the emphasis of each.

Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Move"
We packed the house into brown boxes,
even the smell of the old front hall.
My mother says home is the people,
but the empty rooms still call.

STORY: Jordan walked through the apartment one last time. His footsteps echoed now that the furniture was gone. In his old bedroom, a faint rectangle on the wall marked where his poster had hung for six years. His dad appeared in the doorway with the last box. "Ready?" Jordan touched the bare wall once, then nodded. "Yeah," he said, though his throat felt tight.

Both texts present the same experience. Explain how the poem and the story each create the feeling of leaving a home.
items.answer: The poem creates the feeling of leaving home through compressed images and a stated tension, packing 'even the smell of the old front hall' and the line 'the empty rooms still call,' which name the pull of the place in a few words. The story creates the same feeling through small sensory details and action, the echoing footsteps, the faded rectangle where the poster hung, and Jordan's tight throat. The poem states the conflict between people and place, while the story shows it through what Jordan sees and does.

steps: Identify the shared experience: both texts show the ache of leaving a home.
Poem's method: condensed images ('the smell of the old front hall') and the direct line 'the empty rooms still call' name the feeling quickly.
Story's method: concrete sensory detail (echoing steps, the faded rectangle, the tight throat) builds the feeling through scene and action.
A complete answer contrasts the poem's stated, compressed feeling with the story's shown, detailed feeling.

Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Practice"
The ball goes up, the ball comes down,
a thousand times the same dull arc.
No crowd, no clock, no shining cup,
just me and the rim in the dark.

STORY: Long after the other dancers had gone home, Mei stayed in the empty studio. The mirror showed only her, repeating the same eight counts again and again, fixing the turn that kept going wrong. There was no music now, just the squeak of her shoes and the count under her breath. She would get it right, even if no one ever saw the hundred tries it took.

Both texts share a theme about hidden effort. Name one way the texts are similar, with evidence from each.
items.answer: Both texts share the idea that real skill is built through lonely, unseen repetition. The poem shows the speaker shooting 'a thousand times the same dull arc' with 'no crowd, no clock, no shining cup,' alone in the dark. The story shows Mei repeating the same eight counts in an empty studio 'even if no one ever saw the hundred tries it took.' Each text stresses effort that happens without any audience.

steps: Find the shared theme: skill comes from solitary, unseen practice.
Poem evidence: 'a thousand times the same dull arc' and 'No crowd, no clock, no shining cup' show repetition with no audience.
Story evidence: Mei repeats the counts alone 'even if no one ever saw the hundred tries it took.'
A complete answer states the shared theme of hidden effort and quotes the matching idea from each text.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "The Map"
Grandfather kept the country folded
in a drawer, in a worn-soft square.
He never went back to the streets he drew,
but he kept them, just to know they were there.

STORY: Aunt Rosa cooked the same stew every Sunday, the one from the village she left at nineteen. She had not seen that village in forty years. "The recipe is all I carried out," she told Leo as she stirred. "As long as the kitchen smells like this, a little of home is still here." Leo realized the stew was not just food. It was a way of keeping a place she could not return to.

Both texts explore memory and home. Explain how each form shapes the way it presents holding onto a lost place.
items.answer: The poem shapes its idea through a single concrete object and quiet lines, the folded map kept 'just to know they were there,' which makes holding on feel still and private. The story shapes the same idea through a repeated action and dialogue, Rosa's weekly stew and her line 'a little of home is still here,' which makes holding on feel ongoing and sensory through smell and routine. The poem fixes the memory in one kept object, while the story keeps it alive through a habit the reader can almost taste.

steps: Identify the shared topic: both texts show a person holding onto a home they cannot return to.
Poem's form: one symbolic object, the folded map kept 'just to know they were there,' presents memory as a quiet, fixed keepsake.
Story's form: a repeated action (the Sunday stew) and dialogue present memory as a living, sensory routine.
A complete answer connects the poem's single object to its stillness and the story's repeated action to its ongoing, sensory feel.

Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Speak"
I had the words lined up like soldiers,
brave in my head, in a neat straight row.
But when the room turned to look at me,
they scattered, and would not go.

STORY: Devon had rehearsed his speech for the class election a hundred times. Yet when he reached the podium and saw every face turn toward him, his careful notes blurred. He gripped the edges of the stand. Then he set the cards down, took a breath, and just spoke from the heart about why he cared. It was messier than his script, but people leaned in.

Both texts show the same struggle. Name one difference in how each text resolves the moment of fear.
items.answer: Both texts show the fear of speaking in front of others, but they resolve it differently. The poem ends in defeat, with the speaker's words that 'scattered, and would not go,' so the fear wins. The story ends in recovery, because Devon sets down his cards, breathes, and 'just spoke from the heart,' so he pushes through and 'people leaned in.' The poem leaves the fear unresolved while the story shows the character overcome it.

steps: Identify the shared struggle: stage fright when speaking before a group.
Poem's resolution: the words 'scattered, and would not go,' so the moment ends in failure.
Story's resolution: Devon recovers, speaks 'from the heart,' and the audience leans in, so the moment ends in success.
A complete answer names the same fear but contrasts the poem's defeat with the story's recovery.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Wolf Pup"
They called him wild, they called him wrong,
the gray one slow to learn the rules.
But he heard the far-off howl first,
and led the lost ones home through pools.

STORY: Ben was always the kid who could not sit still, the one teachers sighed about. On the overnight field trip, when fog rolled in and two classmates lost the trail, it was Ben who noticed the faint sound of the river and remembered which way it flowed. He guided the group back while the careful, rule-following students stood frozen. Sometimes the restless mind sees what the still one misses.

Both texts share a theme. Explain how each form develops the idea that a different kind of mind can be a strength.
items.answer: Both texts develop the idea that someone seen as difficult or different can have a hidden strength. The poem develops it through a wolf as a symbol and a turn in the lines: the pup 'called wild' and 'slow to learn the rules' is the one who 'heard the far-off howl first' and 'led the lost ones home.' The story develops it through a realistic scene, restless Ben who cannot sit still becoming the one who hears the river and guides the group home. The poem uses an animal symbol and a quick reversal, while the story uses a true-to-life event.

steps: Identify the shared theme: a mind that does not fit the rules can become a real strength.
Poem's development: the wolf pup symbol and the reversal where the 'wild' one leads the lost ones home carry the theme through image.
Story's development: a realistic event, Ben noticing the river and guiding the group, carries the same theme through plot.
A complete answer names the shared theme and contrasts the poem's symbolic reversal with the story's realistic event.

Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Letting Go"
I held the kite string until my hand burned,
sure that to hold was to keep it mine.
But the kite only flew when I opened my fist.
Some things grow truest past the line.

STORY: Mrs. Okafor watched her daughter Ada pack for college. She wanted to fold every shirt, double-check every box, ride along to the dorm. Instead she handed Ada the keys to the loaded car and stepped back. "You drive," she said, though her hands itched to take over. Ada grinned and started the engine. Mrs. Okafor stood in the driveway and let her go, and felt, beneath the ache, a quiet pride.

Both texts explore the same idea. State the shared theme and explain how each text's form delivers it.
items.answer: Both texts explore the idea that loving someone or something can mean letting it go free. The poem delivers it through the kite metaphor and a clear lesson, 'the kite only flew when I opened my fist,' which states the idea in a single image. The story delivers it through a parent-and-child scene, Mrs. Okafor handing over the keys and feeling 'a quiet pride' beneath the ache, which shows the same idea through a real choice. The poem teaches the lesson with a symbol while the story lives it through action.

steps: Name the shared theme: real love or care sometimes means releasing what you want to hold onto.
Poem's delivery: the kite metaphor and the line 'the kite only flew when I opened my fist' state the lesson through image.
Story's delivery: Mrs. Okafor handing over the keys and feeling 'a quiet pride' shows the same idea through a parent's choice.
A complete answer names the shared theme and contrasts the poem's metaphor with the story's enacted scene.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Bench"
My grandmother's hands were maps of work,
lined deep with every garden, every loaf.
She never told her stories out loud,
but her hands wrote them, soft on soft.

STORY: Tariq did not understand why his father kept the old, dented toolbox when he could afford new tools. Then one afternoon his father opened it and named each worn item: the hammer from his first job, the wrench his own father had used, the level he bought the week Tariq was born. "These are not just tools," his father said. "They are the days I worked to get us here." Tariq looked at the toolbox differently after that.

Both texts share a topic. Name one way they are similar in how they treat that topic, with evidence from each.
items.answer: Both texts are similar because each treats ordinary objects or hands as carriers of a person's whole life of work and love. The poem shows the grandmother's hands as 'maps of work' that 'wrote' her untold stories, so her labor holds her history. The story shows the father's worn tools, the hammer, the wrench, the level, as 'the days I worked to get us here,' so the objects hold his history too. Both texts find a life's story in everyday things tied to hard work.

steps: Find the shared topic: everyday objects or hands can hold the story of a person's lifetime of work.
Poem evidence: the grandmother's hands are 'maps of work' that 'wrote' stories she never spoke.
Story evidence: the father's worn tools are 'the days I worked to get us here.'
A complete answer states the similarity and quotes the matching idea from each text.

Read the poem, then the drama excerpt.

POEM: "Witness"
I saw the bigger kid take the ball,
and I looked away, I will not lie.
The silence after was the loudest thing,
louder than any reason why.

DRAMA:
[The lunchroom. ROSA sees MARCUS knock TONY's lunch tray to the floor and walk off laughing. Other students look down at their food.]
ROSA (standing): That was not okay, Marcus. Pick it up.
MARCUS: Or what?
ROSA: Or everyone here knows what you did. (She kneels and starts gathering Tony's food. After a beat, two other students kneel to help.)

These two texts are in different forms but share a topic. Explain how the poem and the drama each present the choice to act or stay silent.
items.answer: The poem presents the choice through a single regretful voice looking back, the speaker who 'looked away' and felt 'the silence after was the loudest thing,' so it shows the cost of staying silent from the inside. The drama presents the same choice through live action and dialogue, Rosa standing up, telling Marcus 'That was not okay,' and kneeling to help, with stage directions showing others join in. The poem shows silence and its regret, while the drama shows the opposite choice unfolding in real time on stage.

steps: Identify the shared topic: the choice to speak up or stay silent when you see someone treated unfairly.
Poem's form: a lone first-person voice in regret, 'I looked away' and 'the silence after was the loudest thing,' shows the inner cost of staying quiet.
Drama's form: dialogue and stage directions show Rosa acting, standing, speaking, and kneeling, with others following.
A complete answer contrasts the poem's inward regret over silence with the drama's outward, acted-out choice to speak up.

Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Race"
The fast one sprinted, sure to win,
and mocked the slow one's plodding feet.
But steady steps outlast a boast,
and pride trips up its own conceit.

STORY: Carlos finished his book report in twenty minutes and bragged about how easy it was. Nia took two weeks, reading the book twice and revising her draft four times. On presentation day, Carlos stumbled over facts he had not really learned, while Nia spoke clearly about details no one else had noticed. The teacher's praise went to the slow, careful work, not the quick, careless boast.

Both texts deliver a similar message. Name one way they are alike and explain how each form carries that message.
items.answer: Both texts deliver the message that steady, careful effort beats quick, boastful work. The poem carries it through a fable-like contrast and a stated moral, 'steady steps outlast a boast, and pride trips up its own conceit.' The story carries it through a realistic classroom example, Carlos finishing in twenty minutes and stumbling, while Nia takes two weeks and earns the praise. The poem states the lesson in rhymed lines, while the story proves it through a believable event.

steps: Find the shared message: patient, careful effort wins out over fast, prideful shortcuts.
Poem's carrying: a fable-style contrast and the stated moral 'steady steps outlast a boast' deliver the lesson directly.
Story's carrying: the realistic example of Carlos and Nia shows the lesson through events and outcome.
A complete answer names the shared message and contrasts the poem's stated moral with the story's worked-out example.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then the story passage.

POEM: "Open Door"
We set one extra plate each night,
for whoever the dark might send.
My father said a stranger fed
leaves the table as a friend.

STORY: When the new student, a quiet boy named Hassan, sat alone at lunch for the third day, Grace did not know his language well. She simply moved her tray to his table and pushed half her cookies toward him. He looked up, surprised, then smiled and shared his own snack. By Friday their table was the loudest in the room, full of kids who had all once eaten alone.

Both texts share a theme about welcome. State the theme, then name one difference in how the two forms develop it.
items.answer: Both texts share the theme that welcoming a stranger turns them into a friend and creates community. They differ in scope and form: the poem develops the theme as a stated family tradition and a general truth, the extra plate set 'for whoever the dark might send' and the father's saying that 'a stranger fed leaves the table as a friend.' The story develops it through one specific friendship that grows outward, Grace sharing cookies with Hassan until 'their table was the loudest in the room.' The poem states a timeless rule, while the story shows the welcome spreading to many over a week.

steps: Name the shared theme: welcoming a stranger can turn them into a friend and build community.
Poem's development: a stated tradition and a general saying, the extra plate and 'a stranger fed leaves the table as a friend.'
Story's development: a single, growing friendship, Grace and Hassan, that expands until the table is full and loud.
A complete answer names the shared theme and contrasts the poem's stated general rule with the story's specific, spreading example.
